articleSummary: Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, is rising in Brazil, despite being ancient and curable. Transmission is mainly through direct contact with infected lesions during sexual activity, with vertical transmission possible, causing congenital syphilis. Disease stages include primary (painless entry ulcer), secondary (dermatologic lesions, including on the palms and soles), and latent (asymptomatic for weeks to years). Diagnosis uses rapid serology (antibody detection) and VDRL titers; interpretation requires exposure history and clinical context. Testing intervals: highly exposed sexually active individuals every six months; others at least annually. Treatment with benzathine penicillin can cure when properly administered; the number of doses depends on the stage and duration of infection. Untreated syphilis can damage organs and facilitate HIV transmission. Public health measures should expand education, including school programs and prenatal testing to prevent congenital syphilis.

articleHeadline: Anvisa approves medication to treat schistosomiasis in children - Diário de Notícias.
articleSummary: Farmanguinhos Arpraziquantel has been registered by Brazil's Anvisa for treating schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma mansoni or Schistosoma haematobium in children from 3 months up to 6 years old. The approval, published in the Diário Oficial da União, marks a new pediatric option against a disease considered a public health problem in tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and South America. When ingested, arpraziquantel is absorbed by the worms in the host's blood vessels, causing muscular spasms and paralysis that disrupt the parasites' attachment to the vasculature. The drug also damages the parasite's tegument, weakening its protective barrier against the immune system and enabling destruction by the host. The move highlights regulatory efforts to combat pediatric schistosomiasis in endemic regions.

articleHeadline: Northwest region accounts for 60% of visceral leishmaniasis cases in São Paulo state.
articleSummary: Visceral leishmaniasis in São Paulo state’s Northwest accounts for about 60% of confirmed cases this year, with 12 of 22 occurrences in the São José do Rio Preto and Araçatuba regions. Recent diagnoses span seven cities, led by Andradina, Votuporanga, Ilha Solteira, and Fernandópolis (two cases, one fatal); isolated cases appear in Birigui, Penápolis, and Castilho. Transmitted by female sandflies, the disease in humans causes prolonged fever, rapid weight loss, anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly, potentially fatal without treatment (historically up to 90% mortality). Dogs are major urban reservoirs, showing severe weight loss, weakness, skin lesions, and long nails. Municipalities are intensifying vector-blocking and active case searches, inspecting neighborhoods around recorded cases. With no human vaccine, prevention focuses on keeping yards clean, removing organic waste, using pet-repellent collars, installing screens, and avoiding nocturnal dog walks. Araçatuba region has a recurrent transmission history; ongoing surveillance is maintained.

articleHeadline: Brazil: More than 58,000 dengue cases reported in São Paulo state
articleSummary: São Paulo state, Brazil, reports 58,683 confirmed dengue cases since the start of the year, with 42 deaths, 30 of which are under investigation. Of cases, 57,402 are dengue fever, 1,180 dengue with warning signs, and 101 are severe dengue. Warning signs include vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, and other symptoms; severe dengue involves shock or respiratory distress, severe bleeding, or severe organ damage. More than 297,000 suspected cases have been ruled out, and 7,256 remain under analysis due to pending tests or clinical-epidemiological criteria. The situation underscores ongoing transmission risk in the state and highlights the need for surveillance and vector-control measures. Data reflect the calendar year up to 04 October 2026.

articleHeadline: Scientists Propose Framework to Test Whether Oropouche Virus Harms Fetuses
articleSummary: Brazil's 2024 re-emergence of Oropouche virus prompted a proposed framework in BMC Infectious Diseases to test for fetal harm. While vertical transmission and adverse fetal outcomes have accumulated in reports, robust causal inference lags. Case reports show Oropouche RNA or antigens in placental/fetal tissues and anti-Oropouche IgM in microcephalic newborns, but active replication in fetal tissue remains unproven. The framework combines molecular diagnostics and histology to prove replication: strand-specific RT-PCR for positive-sense RNA, RNAscope with confocal microscopy, PrimeFlow RNA with flow cytometry, and immunohistochemistry for non-structural proteins. Animal models include mice with intact or impaired interferon signaling (noting prior fetal effects in interferon-deficient contexts), golden hamsters as a potentially permissive model, and non-human primates; intrauterine infection as proof-of-concept, plus intracranial inoculation or embryonated eggs. Emphasizes using diverse lineages, minimal passaging, and gestational timing to assess risk to fetuses.

articleHeadline: Fidson Selected to Expand Influenza Treatment Access, Pandemic Preparedness
articleSummary: Influenza antiviral baloxavir marboxil will be developed as generic versions under MPP's voluntary license with Roche; Fidson Healthcare Plc is selected as one of eleven manufacturers across nine countries to sign sublicences, expanding production across regions including Brazil, China, and India. The move aims to diversify manufacturing capacity and strengthen pandemic preparedness by enabling rapid, quality-assured access to baloxavir. MPP Executive Director Charles Gore said implementation with manufacturers is underway to support product development and regulatory approval to make generics available quickly, combining global capacity with regionally focused production for a geographically diverse, resilient supply base. Roche VP Tamara Schudel called the milestone, noting that voluntary partnerships are critical for pandemic preparedness and rapid response.

articleHeadline: Anti-Dengue Campaign Passes Through 20 Blocks in Portão
articleSummary: Dengue control campaign 'Curitiba sem Mosquito' moves through the Portão Regional in Curitiba, Brazil this week. Health agents conduct on-site educational briefings to explain prevention measures. During the action, they educate residents on dengue prevention and proper disposal of debris, with collection by trucks from the Municipal Secretariat of Environment. The operation covers 20 blocks in the Fazendinha neighborhood. Residents will be advised tomorrow and Wednesday, with collection scheduled for Thursday. For pickup, residents should place debris outside their homes on the day the trucks pass. Residents are urged to participate and ensure debris is placed outside on the designated day to maximize pickup efficiency.
